## Human tetrachromacy {#sec-human-tetrachromacy}

If we hold "tetrachromacy" to the strict **Grassmann–Maxwell standard**—meaning an observer who requires **four independent primaries** in a color-matching experiment and rejects trichromatic metamers across the visible spectrum (**"strong"** or **functional tetrachromacy**) (Jordan & Mollon, 1993; Jordan & Mollon, 2019)—the honest answer is that **behavioral evidence is surprisingly sparse** (Jordan & Mollon, 2019).

While roughly 12–15% of women are *retinal* tetrachromats (heterozygous carriers of anomalous trichromacy who express four distinct cone opsins in their retinal mosaic due to random X-chromosome inactivation), the overwhelming majority are behaviorally trichromatic (Jordan et al., 2010; Jordan & Mollon, 2019). However, there are **three foundational psychophysical papers** (appropriately enough, two of them led by **John Mollon** and **Gabriele Jordan**) that tested this directly using color-matching and Rayleigh-region metamerism rather than just genetics.

---

### 1. The Most Convincing Behavioral Paper: Jordan, Deeb, Bosten, & Mollon (2010)

The single most rigorous psychophysical demonstration of functional tetrachromacy in the literature is **Jordan et al. (2010)** in the *Journal of Vision*.

Instead of asking observers to adjust four knobs across the full spectrum (which is notoriously noisy), Jordan and Mollon simplified the linear algebra by restricting the stimuli to the **Rayleigh region ($\ge 546\text{ nm}$)**, where S-cones are completely insensitive (Jordan & Mollon, 1993; Jordan & Mollon, 2019):

* **The Dimensionality Reduction:** In the $\ge 546\text{ nm}$ spectral range, a normal trichromat only has two active cone classes ($L$ and $M$) and is therefore reduced to a **dichromat**—meaning they can match *any* monochromatic test light (e.g., $589\text{ nm}$ yellow) using a linear mixture of just **two primaries** ($546\text{ nm}$ green and $670\text{ nm}$ red) (Jordan & Mollon, 2019).
* **The Tetrachromat Prediction:** A woman who expresses three long/middle-wave cones ($L, L', M$) and preserves all three signals post-receptorally is a **trichromat in the Rayleigh region** (Jordan et al., 2010). Therefore, she should **never** accept a two-primary match: for *any* ratio of $546\text{ nm} + 670\text{ nm}$ and *any* radiance of $589\text{ nm}$, the two fields will never equate all three cone excitations simultaneously (Jordan & Mollon, 2019).
* **The Forced-Choice Color-Matching Test:** To eliminate subjective criterion bias ("is this a close enough match?"), Jordan et al. (2010) used a 3-alternative oddity forced-choice task across systematically varied red-green ratios and luminances (Jordan & Mollon, 2019). Every trichromatic control failed to discriminate the mixture from the monochromatic light at their personal Rayleigh match point (Jordan & Mollon, 2019).
* **The Result (Subject `cDa29`):** Out of **24 obligate female carriers** of deuteranomaly (and 7 carriers of protanomaly), **only one woman—subject `cDa29**`—was able to discriminate the red-green mixture from the monochromatic standard at *every single ratio and intensity*, exhibiting zero matching range and fast response times right through the normal metamer point (Jordan et al., 2010; Jordan & Mollon, 2019). She also separated stimuli along an extra dimension in a surface-color multidimensional scaling (MDS) task designed to be metameric for normal trichromats (Jordan et al., 2010).

---

### 2. The Four-Channel Colorimeter Paper: Jordan & Mollon (1993)

Prior to the 2010 forced-choice paper, **Jordan & Mollon (1993)** built a four-channel Maxwellian-view colorimeter to test **ratio matches** in 31 female carriers of color deficiency (Jordan & Mollon, 1993).

* **The Experiment:** Observers adjusted the ratio of a mixture of **$546\text{ nm} + 600\text{ nm}$** to match a mixture of **$570\text{ nm} + 690\text{ nm}$** (alongside standard large-field $10^\circ$ Rayleigh matches) (Jordan & Mollon, 1993).
* **The Geometry:** For a normal trichromat (who is dichromatic in this long-wave regime), the spectrum locus from $546\text{ nm}$ to $690\text{ nm}$ collapses onto a 1D straight line in chromaticity space, meaning there is a whole continuum of matches (Jordan & Mollon, 1993). For a functional tetrachromat (who is trichromatic in this regime), the spectrum locus curves in a 2D plane; the two mixture lines intersect at only a **single unique point ($M$)** (Jordan & Mollon, 1993).
* **The Finding:** Several heterozygous women reported that they were **unable to obtain a perfect match at any ratio** on the standard two-primary Rayleigh match, and one carrier showed the tight, unique intersection point predicted for a tetrachromat on the four-wavelength ratio match (Jordan & Mollon, 1993). It was in this paper that Jordan and Mollon introduced the crucial distinction between **"weak tetrachromacy"** (four retinal cone types projected down to three post-receptoral neural channels) and **"strong tetrachromacy"** (four independent neural signals requiring four primaries) (Jordan & Mollon, 1993; Jordan & Mollon, 2019).

---

### 3. The Chromatic Adaptation / Additivity Failure Paper: Nagy, MacLeod, Heyneman, & Eisner (1981)

If you want to illustrate **Grassmann's Laws breaking down** in female carriers ("weak tetrachromacy"), the classic paper is **Nagy et al. (1981)** in *JOSA*.

* **The Color-Matching Test:** Nagy and MacLeod measured large-field Rayleigh matches in heterozygous women before and after adapting the retina to bright red or blue backgrounds (and after photopigment bleaches) (Nagy et al., 1981).
* **What They Found:** These women were **trichromatic** under any single steady state (they accepted a normal three-primary match, or a two-primary Rayleigh match) (Nagy et al., 1981). However, unlike normal male and female trichromats whose matches remained invariant under chromatic adaptation (Persistence of Metamers / Grassmann's proportionality law), **four of the heterozygous women showed significant additivity failure**: their Rayleigh match midpoints shifted systematically depending on whether the adapting background was red or blue (Nagy et al., 1981).


* **Why This Happens Linear-Algebraically:** Even when a carrier’s cuatro-cone mosaic ($S, M, L', L$) is pooled into just **three** post-receptoral ganglionic channels (so her perceptual space is 3D), nonlinear gain control (von Kries adaptation) acts on the **four** cone classes individually *before* they are summed (Nagy et al., 1981; Jordan & Mollon, 2019). Thus, selectively adapting $L$ vs. $L'$ alters the effective spectral sensitivity of the pooled channel and breaks the metamerism (Nagy et al., 1981; Danilova & Mollon, 2022).

---

### Why Is Functional ("Strong") Tetrachromacy So Rare?

As **Jordan & Mollon (2019)** summarize in their retrospective review, there are two main reasons why almost all women with four cone genes still behave like trichromats in color-matching experiments:

1. **Spectral Separation ($\Delta \lambda_{\max}$):** In most carriers of deuteranomaly, the hybrid $L'$ pigment is only separated from the normal $L$ pigment by $2\text{--}6\text{ nm}$. Their star tetrachromat subject `cDa29` happened to inherit a rare hybrid allele with an estimated **$12\text{ nm}$ separation** between her $L'$ and $L$ cones, giving her three well-spaced pigments in the middle-to-long wavelengths ($530\text{ nm}$, $\sim 548\text{ nm}$, and $560\text{ nm}$) (Jordan et al., 2010; Jordan & Mollon, 2019).
2. **The Post-Receptoral Bottleneck & Cortical Learning:** The primate visual system only has two hardwired chromatic opponent pathways (parvocellular $L/M$ midget cells and koniocellular $S/(L+M)$ cells) (Jordan & Mollon, 2019). Even if a foveal midget ganglion cell draws its center from a single $L'$ cone and its surround from local $L + M + L'$ cones, the cortex lives in an environment of man-made trichromatic displays, prints, and color names, and almost always collapses the redundant signals back into a 3D perceptual space unless the spectral separation is unusually large (Jordan & Mollon, 2019).
